## Conclusion

Yes: the evidence reviewed here indicates that a state-level voucher program would expand parental options while producing measurable gains for participating students [1][2][3]. The fiscal case is favourable on the same evidence, because voucher amounts are set below average per-pupil expenditure [4]. The strongest opposing view is that vouchers drain resources from the district schools that most students remain in, and the competitive-effects evidence reviewed below runs against it: test scores of students remaining in nearby public schools rose slightly rather than falling [5]. On the record assembled here the balance favours adoption, with the design caveats noted in the final section.

## Key findings

- A three-state analysis found participating students gained the equivalent of two months of additional learning in reading over two years [1].
- A longitudinal follow-up reported that those gains persisted through middle school for students who remained in the program [2].
- Graduation rates improved by four percentage points among voucher users relative to matched public-school peers [3].
- A fiscal model projects net savings of roughly $1,400 per participating student, because voucher amounts are set below average per-pupil expenditure [4].
- Students remaining in nearby public schools showed small positive test-score effects, consistent with competition improving district performance [5].

## The strongest counterargument

The objection with the most political weight is that a voucher program is a transfer out of the district system: every departing student takes funding with them, fixed costs do not fall proportionally, and the students who remain — disproportionately those with the least capacity to move — are left in a school with a smaller budget. Stated at full strength, the claim is that measured gains for participants are purchased from non-participants, and that a study of participants alone cannot detect the price.

The competitive-effects evidence is what answers it. Analysis of the districts nearest to participating schools found small positive effects on the test scores of students who remained, not the declines the objection predicts [5]. The fiscal analysis points the same way: because the voucher is set below per-pupil expenditure, the district retains a share of the funding for a student it no longer educates, which is the mechanism that makes a positive competitive effect affordable [4]. What would have to hold for the conclusion to flip is a decline in outcomes for non-participants large enough to outweigh the participant gains in [1] and [3]; nothing in the record assembled here reports one.

## Achievement effects

A 2022 analysis by {{advocacy_org}} of three state programs found participating students gained the equivalent of two months of additional learning in reading over two years [1]. The same organization's longitudinal follow-up reported that gains persisted through middle school for students who remained in the program, with the largest effects among students who entered before third grade [2].

A study published in {{journal_name}} estimated graduation-rate improvements of four percentage points among voucher users relative to matched public-school peers, using administrative records rather than survey data [3].

The three results are consistent in direction and roughly consistent in magnitude once the different outcome measures are put on a common scale [1][3]. Two months of reading growth over two years and a four-point graduation difference are the kind of effects that compound if they persist, which is what the follow-up in [2] was designed to test.

## Fiscal impact

{{advocacy_org}}'s fiscal model projects net savings to the state of roughly $1,400 per participating student, because voucher amounts are set below average per-pupil expenditure [4]. The model attributes additional savings to reduced capital costs as enrollment shifts away from districts operating below capacity.

Savings of that kind are contingent on take-up: a program used mainly by families already in private schools converts an existing private payment into a public one and produces no offsetting district saving [4].

## Effects on public schools and program design

Analysis in {{journal_name}} found small positive competitive effects on the test scores of students remaining in nearby public schools, consistent with the view that competition improves district performance [5].

Two design choices carry most of the risk. An income cap determines whether the program funds new access or subsidises existing private enrollment, and the fiscal case in [4] assumes the former. Testing and reporting requirements for participating schools determine whether the achievement effects in [1] and [3] can be verified at all outside the evaluations cited here.
